newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai property firms face cash crunch - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Thai property firms face cash crunch - Salomon.

text.p: A number of property companies in Thailand were struggling to deal with an oversupply and some were raising cash aggressively to meet their obligations, Salomon Brothers said on Friday.
"Bangkok Land's fragile financial condition is apparent despite its considerable asset holdings in Bangkok," Salomon analyst Juanita Mayr said in a research report.
The company had been scrambling for cash longer than other Thai property firms, but its situation had eased recently with the signing of two government contracts valued at about 4.8 billion baht.
"Cash is still desperately needed not only to pay bills but also for project development that can no longer be delayed," Mayr said.
Contracts of about 5 billion baht would be needed to redeem the company's outstanding 9.1 billion baht in Euro-convertible bonds, Mayr said.
Salomon said two property companies which were weak were Juldis and Property Perfect.
"To meet its cash shortfall of about 200 million baht in 1997, (Juldis) has started to sell assets aggressively, including some long-term holdings," Mayr said.
But she believed the company would overcome "this extremely difficult period" with or without government help thanks to an extensive business and contacts network.
Property Perfect also had a very high risk profile, Salomon said, adding that its policy of leveraging its balance sheet through high capital expenditure seemed to have stretched the company.

"Having already exhausted its borrowing capacity when business was good and financing was easy it will have tremendous difficulties in refinancing those debt issues maturing in today's market," Mayr wrote.
Siam Syntech seemed to have a brighter future, with the company poised for growth despite market weakness, she said.

Siam Syntech had reduced its exposure to risky projects and clients and expanded into neighbouring countries where margins and profits were higher. Its internal cash flow was also high enough to cover all operating expenses.

Another company, MDX, used valuable power projects to borrow large amounts and secure a high cash balance, but concern about future cash flow suggested the company's US$80 million convertible bond "may not suit the risk profile of many investors."

Tanayong dealt with the slump by maintaining a selective approach to property projects while proceeding steadily with the construction of the Bangkok mass transit project, ensuring stable performance for the foreseeable future.

Salomon rated Hemaraj best of the seven mentioned in its report. It said Hemaraj enjoyed a healthy cash position despite domestic sluggishness thanks to land sales to foreign investors and steady expansion into businesses with recurrent earnings.
According to Salomon, default risk was not limited to property companies, but also extended to the financial sector.

"Liquidity for some companies is diminished further whenever the baht weakens due to a high reliance on U.S. dollar funding," the report said. The Thai baht was recently fixed at a 10-1/2 year low of 26.10 to the U.S. dollar.
The report was written following Somprasong Land's default on interest payments on its Euro-convertible bond and the forced merger between Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank.
